anchors.fact: In 1824 Samuel Morewood wrote that the traveller Engelbert Kämpfer had credited the spirit's discovery to "Professor Sylvius of Leiden". Through that essay the attribution entered mainstream drinks history. (A1; F2-F3; Oxford SYLVIUS pdf 1968)
anchors.meaning: The neat answer arrived complete: a name, a title, a city. Leiden is Morewood's word, not the narrator's (G2).
anchors.speaksTo: essence: being fooled by an easy answer

anchors.fact: Oxford calls Morewood the founder of the field and his essay pioneering; it held the first comprehensive history of distilling, and some of its sections haven't been entirely replaced since. He was probably right that the spirit Kämpfer named was ordinary genever. (A2; F2, F4, F7; pdf 1968, SPIRITS WRITING pdf 1884)
anchors.meaning: The answer came from the most careful person in the room, who got the hard part right. Grant him before anything else (Wren b). Keep "probably".
anchors.speaksTo: Sage goal: Wisdom · Wren (2): someone careful, not a fool

anchors.fact: Kämpfer seems to have meant Sylvius's own version of the traditional Dutch spirit; Morewood took it to mean Sylvius fathered the spirit itself. (A3; F6, F8; pdf 1968) What the 1691 conversation was about stays out (G1), and Kämpfer did call the spirit newly invented, so never "he never said so" (G3).
anchors.meaning: Going back to what was actually said makes the claim smaller: one man's recipe, not the spirit. The second look narrows the name; it doesn't swap in a new one (C3). "Seems" stays in the reading.
anchors.speaksTo: story: the truth is always one layer deeper · Wren (4)

anchors.fact: Most nineteenth- and twentieth-century writers followed him without question; he is still cited so widely that historians despair of removing the title, and they have only recently begun to correct it. (A4; F1, F9; pdf 1968)
anchors.meaning: It held because it was satisfying. That motive is not on the page: "I like to think" only. No span of years in the epigraph (Wren f); "most", never "everyone" (G4).

anchors.fact: Genever goes back at least to the late 1400s. A 1495 Dutch cookbook by an unknown, clearly wealthy author has a recipe seen as the first mention of a juniper spirit drunk for pleasure: distilled wine with the costliest spices of the day, juniper one of the cheap ones. Sylvius was born in 1614. (A5; F10-F11; pdf 1968, GENEVER pdf 872-873)
anchors.meaning: Under the one name is something older and bigger, from more than a century before him. The author's name is unknown: one clause at most, never the landing (Wren a; G7).
anchors.speaksTo: position: what's underneath is older and bigger (Wren r1)

anchors.fact: That early spirit was distilled from wine; by 1588 grain had replaced grapes. Today's genever is built on malt wine, a grain spirit distilled at least three times. (A6; F12, F17; pdf 570, 873-874)
anchors.meaning: The glass holds the grain descendant, not the 1495 recipe: never "the same spirit" or "the original" (Tomás's fence).

anchors.fact: After a Dutch king took the English throne in 1688, English distillers copied genever without its grain or skill, made up the flavour with more botanicals and sugar, and shortened the name too: "geneva", from jenever, became "gin". (A7; F13; GENEVER pdf 873, GIN pdf 890)
anchors.meaning: The short, familiar word sits on top of the older spirit; the guest's glass holds the elder. Not "stripped" (*Half a Rim*).
anchors.speaksTo: Wren r1: the older, bigger thing under the neat name

anchors.fact: Oude ("old") genever must hold at least 15% malt wine, at most 20 g sugar a litre, at least 35% ABV; no genever has to be aged, whatever it's called. After 1945 the lighter jonge style almost killed oude off; the cocktail revival since the 1990s brought it back. (A8; F15-F16; pdf 874-875)
anchors.meaning: Even "old" is an easy answer: it means the older style, not years in a barrel. Never "aged" (G6). Tomás's to use or not.

anchors.fact: Holland gin and brandy were by far the most popular spirits for the early Cocktail (the page sits beside an 1833 recipe). By the 1880s drinkers were asking for cocktails the "old-fashioned" way, with spirit, lump sugar and ice and nothing added (the 1882 Chicago report names whisky). In 1895 the New York bartender George Kappeler printed it as sugar, two dashes of Angostura, ice, lemon peel and spirit, with a Holland gin version among others. Dutch gin began to disappear from American bars with the Dry Martini in the 1890s. (A9; F14, F18; *Imbibe!* pdf 68, 175, 185-187; GENEVER pdf 874; v2: the early-Cocktail popularity and the 1880s requests are two eras, never one sentence)
anchors.meaning: The plain build is how this spirit was drunk before it went out of fashion.
anchors.speaksTo: drink: the build isn't a bridge

anchors.fact: Caspar Coolhaes (1536-1615) took a professorship at Leiden in 1574, became a distiller after his excommunication in 1582, and in 1588 wrote the earliest known book to confirm grain had replaced grape, disapproving of the change. (A10; F19; COOLHAES pdf 570)
anchors.meaning: There was a Leiden professor in genever's real story, and he grumbled about the very change that made it. **Fence:** never "the real inventor"; offering him as the answer is Morewood's step again (C3). Wren's call; dossier by default.

cocktail.closingLine: The brandy goes in before the genever. Love the next neat idea, then learn what it started as.
cocktail.glassware: rocks glass (about 300 ml), filled with ice cubes
method: Pour the brandy into the rocks glass first.
Add the syrup and the bitters, then pour the genever on top.
Give it a quick stir, fill the glass with ice cubes, and stir again for about 20 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels cold.
Squeeze the lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Look Again

recipe.note: any VS cognac or Armagnac, about 40%. It goes in first
Dutch or Belgian: look for "oude" on the label, not "jonge" (young). "Oude" means the older, maltier style, not aged. 35% or stronger
2 parts sugar to 1 part water, by weight, stirred until clear

cocktail.tagline: The more you like an answer, the harder you look at it.

reading.epigraph: "Gin" began as a short form of the name of the spirit in this glass.
whoYouAre: Over dinner, a friend explains a lovely theory about how something famous really began. It's neat, it has a name and a date in it, and you love it at once. Hours later you're still in your chair, turning it over. People take that for doubt. It's closer to the reverse: you fall for ideas faster than anyone you know, which is exactly why you check the ones you love.

What worries you is your own delight: a lovely idea, passed on with confidence, that turns out to be wrong. And when a favourite doesn't survive a closer look, you let it go without a fuss. Nobody sees what that costs you.

You take other people's ideas as seriously as your own. Someone floats a half-thought, and you follow it further than they dared, and they leave feeling cleverer than they came. It's respect, and it means more to them than you know.
yours: There's a famous answer to who invented gin, repeated so widely that drinks historians despair of ever shifting it: a chemist in Holland called Sylvius. It took hold in 1824, when Samuel Morewood wrote that a German traveller, Engelbert Kämpfer, had credited the spirit's discovery to "Professor Sylvius of Leiden". Morewood was nobody's fool. He's been called the founder of the field, and his history of distilling was the first full one. He was probably right, too, that the spirit Kämpfer meant was genever, the Dutch spirit gin grew out of.

Maybe Sylvius did make a fine one. Kämpfer seems to have meant just that: Sylvius's own version of a spirit the Dutch were already making. Morewood read it as the invention of the spirit itself, and most of the writers who came after him took his word without question. Historians have only recently begun to correct it. Genever goes back at least to the late 1400s, more than a century before Sylvius was born, and the author of its earliest known recipe is unknown.

I like to think the answer lasted because it was such a good one: a name, a title, a city. It's exactly the kind of answer you'd love. And you're also the one who'd go back to the traveller's words late at night, and find the claim smaller than it looked, and the spirit under it older and bigger. I see both of those people in you: the one who loves the neat answer, and the one who goes back anyway.

So the cocktail I've made for you is built on the older spirit. It's that classic of classics, the Old-Fashioned, made after a New York bartender's recipe of 1895, which came in a Holland gin version too: a little sugar, Angostura, lemon peel, ice. The spirit is oude genever, the old style (the word names the style, not years in a barrel): rich, malty, closer to a whisky than to the gin you know, which took its short name from it. Under it, poured in before the genever, is a little French grape brandy, distilled from wine, as a nod to the wine Dutch distillers made their spirit from before they turned to grain. Once it's stirred you can't find the layers. The older one is in every sip.

So keep loving the neat answers. Don't change that. Just, next time one delights you, don't save the going back for midnight and your own chair. Go back with the friend who brought it: "I love that. Want to see what's underneath?" Most of the time, what the two of you find is older and bigger than the story you started with, and it's theirs to keep too. Going back stops being the lonely part, and becomes what the evening was for.
